content: I signed up for a 50K trail race in June — it's in the Cascades so there's going to be significant elevation gain. I've been running 30-40 mile weeks on road but I need to shift to trail training.

For a 50K in the Cascades you'll want to prioritize elevation training and technical trail skills over pure mileage. Time on feet matters more than distance at that point. How much elevation gain does the race have?

About 6,500 feet of gain over the 50K. The course has a mix of single track, fire roads, and one rocky ridge section. The thing is, I live in a pretty flat area so I'll need to find creative ways to train for the elevation.

Stair repeats and treadmill incline work can partially substitute for real hills. Some runners also use a weighted vest on flat trails to simulate the effort of climbing. For the technical sections, find the rockiest trails you can access for weekend long runs.

I've been doing stair repeats at the parking garage near work — 8 floors, 10 repeats. It's boring but effective. For the long runs I drive an hour to the state park that has decent single track with some roots and rocks. I'd rather optimize the training than suffer on race day.
Smart approach. You might also want to practice hiking the steeps — at those grades and that distance, power hiking the climbs is faster and more efficient than trying to run everything.

Yeah, I've been reading about the run-hike strategy for ultras. Fundamentally it's about energy management over the full distance — optimize for total time, not per-mile pace. Same as capacity planning for a distributed system — you can't run every service at 100% CPU.
